this_week.blurb: One year to five. The age that will not keep a dressing on, cannot reliably tell you where it hurts, and puts things in places it would not occur to you to look — and the age at which a great deal of what we were taught turns out to have been someone's reasonable worry, hardened into a rule.

pages.title: The postneonatal infant — 29 days to one year
In an infant, the parent is the monitor
A unit for the first year of life
The postneonatal infant, in three tiers
Fifteen minutes and a well-looking baby
Everything after triage is a disposition
What some of our colleagues have already seen
The newborn generally does not have a cardiac arrest
Cardiac Drugs: Vasopressors and Inotropic Agents
In the immunosuppressed, the absence of signs is the sign
Everyone means to be a donor
PEM Myths
pages.blurb: Seven pieces of paediatric dogma examined — prophylactic atropine, opioids in the acute abdomen, bolusing dextrose, how long to watch after adrenaline, sickle cell trait, steroids for sore throat, and the dressing that cost a two-year-old two fingers.

pages.title: What we monitor, and what we actually know
pages.blurb: The first expert consensus on haemodynamic monitoring in children — and an unusually honest account of how little sits underneath it. Including the gap that matters most here: no agreed blood pressure target under twelve.

pages.title: The toddler and preschool child
pages.blurb: One to five years — when the physiology stops being the hard part and the child becomes it. The airway, the circulation that still lies, croup and wheeze, the foreign body and the button battery, drowning, and the numbers to have written down.

pages.title: Be wary of the toddler who readily and happily lets you examine them
pages.blurb: Objecting to a stranger costs energy, breath and an intact conscious state. A toddler who has none to spare is easy to examine — and we write that down as cooperative.

pages.title: The toddler and preschool child
pages.blurb: Twenty clues from the fortnight — croup, the inhaled peanut, the button battery and what to give while you wait, the burn, and the child who will not let you look. Fill it in on screen, or print it.

pages.title: The twenty minutes either side
pages.blurb: A new series. Practical anaesthesia for the one to five year old — fasting and the runny nose, premedication versus the parent at the head of the bed, the induction, laryngospasm, and the emergence delirium that gets treated as pain.

pages.title: The toddler and preschool child
pages.blurb: One to five years in three tiers — the science of what has changed since infancy, the encounter and how to get anything out of it, and what you will be expected to do on your first nights on call.

pages.title: The toddler and preschool child
pages.blurb: TODDLER — seven things for the one to five year old, from trusting the baseline you are given to reporting what does not fit. The word is the age.

pages.title: Guā shā 刮痧
pages.blurb: A new column, and it opens where it matters most at this age. Gua sha, cupping and moxibustion leave marks that can look like inflicted injury — what they actually look like, and the better question to ask.

pages.title: The Body in Question
pages.blurb: A new column. Jonathan Miller, 1978 — we have almost no access to our own interiors, so every culture has built the body out of whatever machinery was lying around. The metaphor is not decoration. It is the instrument.

pages.title: The toddler and preschool child
pages.blurb: Five open-book questions — the compliant child, the button battery, the inhaled peanut, marks that are not what they look like, and the single thing most likely to make croup worse. Three correct earns a certificate.

pages.title: A small child in intensive care
pages.blurb: A new series, written for anyone rather than for clinicians. What the room contains, what the alarms actually mean, what parents can do — and an open invitation to send any question at all.

pages.title: The child who is not ignoring you
pages.blurb: A new column. Ear disease in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children starts within weeks of birth, usually does not hurt, and takes hearing during the years language is built — which undoes every bedside assessment scored on response.

points: You can register to donate one or more organs and tissues after you die.
Anyone in Australia aged 16 or over can register. You need a Medicare card, and it takes about a minute.
You can change your decision at any time.
If you do not register, your family will be asked to decide for you.
If you do register, tell your family — and ask them to record their own decision too.
